Today I took my sweet time solving, and also changed it up by going across, then down, then back to across and down, filling in what I didn't get on first pass. It was akin to taking a new path from point A to point B, as opposed to the usual one (wherein I do the puzzle in sections, criss-crossing as I go.) Zen masters recommend these tweaks to wake us up from auto-pilot and experience anew being present in the moment. It did make me more focused, brought my attention to the fill, not the end, and afforded me great enjoyment. And this was a perfect puzzle to do that, because the theme and the fill were so good! Thank you, Mr. Cardin! BIRD BY BIRD is new to me and an interesting TIL. Nice to learn bird-by-bird.  One major reason why I do these puzzles is to learn stuff like that.

In my life the same idea has been Q: “How do you eat an elephant?”

A: “One bite at a time.”

Of course we shouldn’t be thinking about eating the remarkable elephants of the world.  They are amazing creatures.

But maybe various species of huge mammals like mammoths and sloths were in North America eaten by our predecessors into extinction.  That and the climate change of 15,000 years ago.

If you were going to make a “word hidden in a phrase” clue for Best-Picture-winner ARGO, could you come up with a more perfect phrase than “and the Oscar goes to…”?

That’s a sweet blast of brilliance.  And then having ARGO crossed with LARGO is the cherry on top.

Nate has a way with finding words masked in phrases.  It was the theme of his last Times puzzle, where names of singers were hidden, such as Elvis in TUNNEL VISION, and the reveal was INSIDE VOICES (as in, what children should use at the library).

That ARGO clue was a highlight for me, bolstered by a supporting cast of lovely answers – PLUCKY, SASHAY, SUBTLY, PHOBIA, BLURTS, and BUOYED.

Beauty and the beast of a clue elevated your puzzle, Nate, above a simple fill-in, and that, sir, elevated my day.  Thank you!

You're right; you're not going to win this one.  I don't have an emotional stake in this process, but I understand:

Descriptivism tells what is happening in an everchanging language.  The only languages that don't change are dead languages.  

Prescriptivism tells what so-called "experts" think should be corrrect.  Often, the reasons behind their decisions are faulty:  we are told not to end a sentence with a preposition because Latin doesn't; we are told not to split an infinitive, again because of Latin, where the infinitive is one word, and as such, cannot be split; we are told not to use certain words or phrases because the wrong crowd uses them.  Prescriptivists are welcome to write style guides for publications so they can set a certain "standard" above what the dictionary allows, but their instructions are arbitrary and voluntary.

And most prescriptivism is practiced by the older generation, because even in the half-century or more they've lived, the language we now have is different from the language our teachers taught us (whose instructions might even have been antiquated back then).

What I can't let go of is double spacing after sentences.  My synapses do not allow me to.  That and AOL email...how do I even start to notify everyone that I'm leaving an antiquated service?

It is precisely the deafness of descriptivism to the flow and change of language over time that makes me nuts. It's not that I ignore change; I love watching it. But descriptivism denies me that.
What descriptivism gives me is, "Today somebody somewhere said XXX and it meant YYY." But where did XXX come from? How does it relate to its source and its social group? Was it derived from an earlier common expression? a shared piece of culture like a song or a dance? A shared history? The revival of an older idea or turn of phrase? How did YYY get attached as its meaning?
Of course, that would require investigation, analysis, thought and consideration.
All descriptivism requires is a data dump. And I mean that exactly the way it sounds.
